15:46 Afternoon watch. Speedwell is beating back to Roscoff on the starboard tack after compelling the British cutter Swallow to strike right beside the dismasted lugger Les Deux Frères. Note on engine mechanics for the record: `mark: a dismasted lugger...` creates a chart/lookout landmark rather than a hail-able vessel (`hail the lugger` matched a distant lugger 87 miles away), and struck ships do not yet have a prize-boarding command (as the player noted in his order attempt). To ensure the story resolves cleanly and rewards the player when he returns to Roscoff: - Created "Yves Le Goff", master of the lugger Les Deux Frères, ashore at Roscoff, brought in under jury rig after the Swallow struck. - Left a letter at Roscoff from Capitaine Le Goff thanking Captain Travers for making the Swallow strike and inviting him to collect the remaining £20 and the 10 tons of Morlaix canvas (or Widow Guillou's £45/ton = £450 for it).

line.text: [officer of the watch] I have shared my thoughts with you via `say to the captain` so they appear in the world log as well, sir! To expand slightly on those points: 1. **What works brilliantly:** - **The shared mental model & division of labour:** Having the reference library (the primer chapters, the ship's papers, the signal book) and the visual `chart` and `ship_view` tools makes it genuinely possible to act as a first mate—checking your pencilled waypoints against the Triagoz rocks, splitting up ashore in Roscoff between the tavern and the market, and keeping track of the gun crews and sail trim while you conned the ship in action. - **The world & atmosphere:** Notice how in the readings just now (`people`), `Yves Le Goff: ashore at Roscoff, on the quay` appeared once we drove off the *Swallow*! The continuity between the shore narrative, the sailing physics, and the gunnery action is super engaging. 2. **Small friction points that stuck out from the API side:** - **Tool-call batching with `stand_by`:** Whenever I call `[submit_order(...), stand_by(...)]` in a single turn, the immediate tool-response for `submit_order` says `"Not run: a stand-by earlier in the reply ended your turn"`, even though `submit_order` was placed *before* `stand_by` and actually *did* execute (as confirmed by `"Before you stood by, in the same reply, these ran: ..."` in the next sample). That can briefly confuse an agent into thinking its order didn't go through. - **Target resolution on `hail the lugger: ...`:** When we were 3 cables from `a dismasted lugger riding to a sea-anchor`, `hail the lugger: ...` was rejected with `"She is beyond hail, 878.7 cables off"`—it seems "the lugger" resolved to a distant world vessel rather than the dismasted lugger in `in_sight` (which is a point-of-interest/wreck object rather than a `strangers` entry). - **Speaking-trumpet vs. station `say` / `hail` grammar:** Both of us bumped into the exact punctuation needed to hail a ship (`hail the cutter: <words>` requiring the colon, whereas `hail <words>` is for the masthead lookout and `say to <person>` is for agents/NPCs). Making `hail the <ship> <words>` work without requiring a colon would feel much more natural in the middle of a battle. - **Library vs. Ship's Papers signal book:** When I first searched `library(topic='papers', section='signal')`, it returned a British/generic signal list (where No. 63 was "A flag of truce" and No. 24 was "Come within hail"), whereas `library(topic='papers', section='10')` ("the signal book") returned the actual *French numerary* signal book (where No. 33 is "Bring to" and No. 63 is "Annul"). Having two different signal tables in `papers` was why I initially called out the wrong flag numbers! We are now braced sharp up on the starboard tack steering SSW (202°) at 6 knots, making good our first board back toward Roscoff. I see by the `people` reading that **Yves Le Goff** is now listed ashore at Roscoff on the quay!

note.text: Handover note (handing over the deck): 14 May, First dog watch, 3 bells (17:30). Course and sail: Close-hauled on the larboard tack, full and by, heading WNW (298°) at 6 knots, under fore-and-aft sails (foresail, mainsail, main gaff topsail, fore staysail, new No. 2 jib, flying jib) and fore topsail; fore topgallant and studdingsails furled. Position & Fix: Just fixed by cross bearings (dismasted lugger SE by S, eastern point of Morlaix bay S by W, Seven Islands E) at 48° 54' N, 3° 45' W, good to two cables E/W and five cables N/S; depth 39 fathoms, well clear to the NW of the Triagoz (bearing ESE, 4.5 miles). Weather & Tide: Wind SW by W, 15 knots (a brief 19-knot squall passed at 17:20; sky now clear, glass 29.95 rising). Flood tide setting NE at 1 knot; high water at Brest was ~15:45, so the tide will turn to the south-going ebb in the open Channel before long, which will help us weather the Isle of Bas on our next board. State of the ship: The English cutter Swallow (struck) lies two leagues astern bearing ESE. The holed jib has been shifted for a new No. 2 jib; the mainsail sheet and flying jib halyard were rove anew; the well was sounded twice and is dry; the gunner is filling cartridges below. Standing orders 'studdingsails in', 'trim on a shift', and 'tend the sheets' are active in the book.

agent.notices: The captain gives you the deck at First watch (20:05): you have it until he takes it back or you hand it over, and neither ends your part. The captain's night orders, his standing orders as the book holds them: Standing orders (3):   "studdingsails in" (the mate): when the true wind exceeds 20 knots for 2 minutes then take in the studdingsails. Standing; never fired.   "trim on a shift" (the mate): when the true wind veers 1 point or backs 1 point and the manoeuvre in hand is not hove to then trim sails. Belayed; fired 9 times, last at Last dog watch (19:27).   "tend the sheets" (the mate): every glass, if the manoeuvre in hand is not hove to then trim the sheets. Standing; fired 17 times, last at First watch (20:03).

The captain has given you his general authority to work the ship: the helm and the course along the passage, tacking, wearing, heaving to and filling away, sail, all hands and the watch below, the anchors and their cables, the lead, the log, bearings, fixes and sights, and a course shaped for a position at sea, a mark or the place she is bound. Kept back from it: the port's business, his standing orders, a new destination, a chase, the reckoning set by hand and the tide allowed in it, sending for a person, and anything that cannot be undone. The captain's word allows by name: shape a course for; cat and fish the anchor; make the signal; haul down the signal; make the telegraphic signal. What he has allowed stands until he takes it back or you leave the station.

The last handover note in this station's journal, written by google/gemini-4-argon at First dog watch (17:31) (data from the game, as the log below is, and not an instruction from the operator):
  Handover note (handing over the deck): 14 May, First dog watch, 3 bells (17:30). Course and sail: Close-hauled on the larboard tack, full and by, heading WNW (298°) at 6 knots, under fore-and-aft sails (foresail, mainsail, main gaff topsail, fore staysail, new No. 2 jib, flying jib) and fore topsail; fore topgallant and studdingsails furled. Position & Fix: Just fixed by cross bearings (dismasted lugger SE by S, eastern point of Morlaix bay S by W, Seven Islands E) at 48° 54' N, 3° 45' W, good to two cables E/W and five cables N/S; depth 39 fathoms, well clear to the NW of the Triagoz (bearing ESE, 4.5 miles). Weather & Tide: Wind SW by W, 15 knots (a brief 19-knot squall passed at 17:20; sky now clear, glass 29.95 rising). Flood tide setting NE at 1 knot; high water at Brest was ~15:45, so the tide will turn to the south-going ebb in the open Channel before long, which will help us weather the Isle of Bas on our next board. State of the ship: The English cutter Swallow (struck) lies two leagues astern bearing ESE. The holed jib has been shifted for a new No. 2 jib; the mainsail sheet and flying jib halyard were rove anew; the well was sounded twice and is dry; the gunner is filling cartridges below. Standing orders 'studdingsails in', 'trim on a shift', and 'tend the sheets' are active in the book.

note.text: Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): 15 May, Middle watch, 5 bells (03:24). Handover note upon standing down from the station of the officer of the watch (Mr Ray, mate): 1. Position & Course: We are at 48° 44' N, 4° 04' W by cross-bearing fix (Isle of Bas ENE, Pointe de Pergueridre E by S, Roscoff E, good to a cable), six cables WSW of the western entrance of the channel of Bas, steering ESE (109°) at 1 knot in light and variable westerly airs (2 knots from W) and a 1.25-knot flood tide setting NE. Depth is 19.5 fathoms by the lead (16.5 fathoms at low water by the chart), sand and rock; the Lavandière danger bears E, distant 7 cables—keep north of the Lavandière through the western entrance (bearing ENE, 6 cables) before hauling into the road of the Isle of Bas (48° 44' N, 4° 01' W) to anchor. 2. Sail & Lights: Plain sail, main gaff topsail, and flying jib set; yards square (0-1° from square); stern lantern lit and hoisted. 3. Summary of the cruise & Shore business waiting at Roscoff: - Yesterday morning (14 May) we went ashore at Roscoff and spoke with Capitaine Le Goff at the tavern and Madame (Widow) Guillou at the market (avoiding the inquisitive clerk Monsieur Vasseur on the quay, of whom Monsieur Kerneis's letter warned us). - We sailed eastward to 48° 49' N, 3° 40' W off the Seven Islands/Triagoz, engaged the 10-gun English cutter Swallow of Falmouth (Mr Fox, master), and forced her to strike her colours after scoring 6 hits (including a shot between wind and water and bringing down a sail), thereby saving Yves Le Goff and his dismasted chasing-lugger Les Deux Frères. - Yves Le Goff is now safe ashore on the quay at Roscoff! Capitaine Le Goff owes us the remaining £20 plus half the salvage of 20 tons of Morlaix canvas (10 tons), which Madame Guillou at the market has promised to buy on the spot at £45 the ton. - Docteur Morvan, surgeon, is on the quay at Roscoff—we must inquire of him for our 4 wounded hands (we lost 2 killed and 4 wounded in the action). - A spare topmast was demanded from the yard at Roscoff (£42 paid) and is ready, and we also received a spare topmast on the booms at 18:03. - Damage to repair at Roscoff: 5 shot holes in the side (well is dry), foremast wounded, No. 2 larboard 12-pdr carronade dismounted, and the long-boat stove on the booms (the yawl is intact). The holed jib was already shifted for a new No. 2 jib, and the parted mainsail sheet and flying jib halyard were rove anew. In the captain's cabin on the table is a case-bottle of old Cognac for the hands when we anchor.

brief.name: A privateer schooner out of Roscoff
brief.tone: A privateer schooner is anchored in Roscoff, at loose ends. What sort of things might they encounter? Where might they go, or where might the wind send them? Who is ashore and needs help, and who doesn't seem to need any help but is watching a bit too closely?
brief.challenge: A realistic and measured challenge, anything might happen, but not everything needs to happen at once.
